title: Longest Shared Subsequence
statement:
You get two strings a and b. A subsequence of a string is what remains after deleting any number of its characters (possibly none) without reordering the rest. The kept characters do not have to be next to each other.

Return the length of the longest string that is a subsequence of both a and b. Return 0 if they share no character.

examples.why: "pary" (or "paty") fits in both. The longest shared contiguous piece is only "pa", so gaps matter.
"more". Greedily matching a's first letter x jumps to the end of b and finds only 1.

constraints: a and b hold lowercase English letters
hints: Compare the last characters of the two strings. Either they match, or at least one of them is not part of the answer.
Let dp[i][j] be the answer for the first i characters of a and the first j of b. If a[i−1] == b[j−1], use both. Otherwise one of them can be dropped. Which two smaller cells does that leave?
dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 on a match, else max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Row 0 and column 0 are 0 (an empty prefix shares nothing). Fill row by row and keep only two rows.

explain.intuition:
dp[i][j] is the length of the longest shared subsequence of the prefixes a[0..i) and b[0..j). Read the recurrence off the last decision: what happens to the last character of each prefix?

If a[i−1] == b[j−1], pair them up. Any shared subsequence that leaves them unpaired can be improved or matched by pairing them, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1. If they differ, they cannot both be the last character of the shared subsequence, so at least one is unused: either skip a's last character, dp[i−1][j], or skip b's, dp[i][j−1]. Take the larger. That is the whole table: match moves diagonally, skip moves up or left.

A greedy walk that matches each letter of a at its first possible spot in b fails because one early match can use up the rest of b, as the x in the third example does. The table tries both "use it" and "skip it" for every pair of prefixes, and each of the (n+1)(m+1) cells is computed once. It is the same idea as a text diff tool: the lines that stay unchanged are a longest shared subsequence.
steps: Make prev, an array of m + 1 zeros: row 0, where a's prefix is empty.
For each i from 1 to n, build cur with cur[0] = 0.
For each j from 1 to m: if a[i−1] == b[j−1], cur[j] = prev[j−1] + 1; otherwise cur[j] = max(prev[j], cur[j−1]).
Set prev = cur. After the last row, return prev[m].
pitfalls: Computing the longest shared substring instead. That resets to 0 on a mismatch and answers 2 for the first example.
Adding 1 on a match to max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]) instead of to the diagonal. That can count one character twice: "a" and "aa" would give 2.
Overwriting a single row in place without saving the diagonal. prev[j−1] must be the value from the row above, which in-place updates have already destroyed; keep it in a variable or use two rows.

solutions.title: Recursion on the last characters
solutions.idea: Compare the last characters: on a match take both, otherwise try dropping either one. No memory, so equal subproblems are solved again and again.

solutions.title: Table over both prefixes
solutions.idea: dp[i][j] for prefixes of length i and j. Match: diagonal + 1. Mismatch: the better of skipping one side.

solutions.title: Two rows
solutions.idea: Each row reads only the row above and itself, so keep the previous row and the current one.

followups: Return one longest shared subsequence itself, not just its length. How do you walk back through the table?
Use the table to list the lines a diff tool would mark as deleted and added between two files.
One string is very long and the other has only distinct characters. Can you turn this into a longest increasing subsequence problem?
